row: Nepal PM to reach Delhi on Sunday for first foreign bilateral trip - what's on agenda

NEW DELHI: Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah will begin a two-day state visit to India on Sunday, his first overseas bilateral state visit since taking office in March."The visit will serve as an important opportunity to review our wide-ranging cooperative partnership with a forward-looking perspective, maximising mutual benefits for the peoples of both countries," Nepal's foreign ministry said in a statement.Shah, an ex-Kathmandu mayor and a former rapper, will be accompanied by a 34-member delegation comprising finance minister Swarnim Wagle, foreign affairs minister Shishir Khanal, his chief advisor Kumar Byanjankar, and other senior government officials.

Balendra Shah's itinerary in New Delhi

Shah is scheduled to hold delegation-level talks with Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Monday, after which they will jointly inaugurate several energy-related projects. The two sides will also sign and exchange bilateral agreements covering various areas of cooperation.The two prime ministers will address a joint press conference, followed by a luncheon hosted by PM Modi in honour of the visiting Nepali leader.During his visit, Shah will also call on President Droupadi Murmu and pay tributes at Mahatma Gandhi's memorial at Rajghat.He is also scheduled to attend the Nepal-India Business Forum, which aims to strengthen trade and economic ties between the two countries.

What's likely to be discussed

According to ministry of external affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal, India and Nepal are expected to discuss issues including development cooperation and people-to-people ties."All these issues will be discussed: development cooperation, people-to-people ties, energy ties, connectivity, and some of the newer areas of cooperation such as startups, technology, innovation, and sports. Cricket links have also become an important connection between India and Nepal.

This is a very important visit for us," Jaiswal told reporters at a weekly news briefing in New Delhi on Friday.Shah is also expected to discuss Indian assistance for the reconstruction of areas affected by the devastating floods in August, Reuters reported, citing Nepalese officials.The August 26 floods killed 1,500 people, left more than 5,200 missing and destroyed roads, bridges, power plants, farms and homes.Nepal is also likely to discuss with India an additional route for commercial flights from the west to Bhairahawa, near Lumbini, the birthplace of Gautam Buddha, and the tourist city of Pokhara.

Karan Manral is a journalist at the Times of India. He covers politics, social issues, and international affairs, exploring stories that affect people’s everyday lives. He also writes explainers to make these stories easier for readers to follow.

row: Who is El Chapo Isidro, the alleged cartel boss arrested in Mexico?
Mexican forces arrested Chapo Isidro in Sinaloa. He was on the FBI’s most wanted list and faces US drug charges.

# Who is El Chapo Isidro, the alleged cartel boss arrested in Mexico?

*Mexican forces arrested Chapo Isidro in Sinaloa. He was on the FBI’s most wanted list and faces US drug charges.*

Mexican special forces have arrested Fausto Isidro Meza-Flores, an alleged cartel leader known as “Chapo Isidro”, who is on the FBI’s Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list, Mexico’s defence ministry said.

Meza-Flores was detained along with two other men on Friday night in Guasave, in the northwestern state of Sinaloa.

The arrest comes as US President Donald Trump has been pressing Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum to do more to combat drug cartels and said on Friday that Washington was working with Sheinbaum “because the cartels are running Mexico.”

“I told her that,” he said. “And we can’t let the cartels run Mexico. They’re our neighbour.”

## Who is Chapo Isidro and what is he accused of?

Despite the similar nickname, Meza-Flores is not related to Joaquin “El Chapo” Guzman, the jailed former leader of the Sinaloa Cartel.

Mexican authorities say Meza-Flores leads the Beltran Leyva criminal organisation and is an ally of the Mayos faction of the Sinaloa Cartel. The Mexican Secretariat of National Defence said he was wanted in Mexico on an arrest warrant for organised crime and drug offences and is subject to an extradition order to the United States.

US prosecutors first indicted Meza-Flores in 2012. In a 2019 indictment, they accused him of conspiring to manufacture and distribute cocaine, heroin, methamphetamine and marijuana for the US market between 2005 and 2019. He also faces a firearms charge.

The FBI added him to its Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list in February 2025, and the US Department of State offered up to $5m for information leading to his arrest and conviction.

“Known as El Chapo Isidro, he’s accused of spending the last 20 years flooding the US with fentanyl, cocaine, heroin, and other deadly drugs, first as an independent drug trafficker and later as the head of the Meza-Flores cartel,” said then-acting FBI Director Brian Driscoll in announcing his addition to the list.

He also said Meza-Flores and his organisation were accused of kidnapping, extortion, torture and murder.

## How was Chapo Isidro arrested?

Mexico’s defence ministry said the operation followed coordination between Mexican and US intelligence agencies and involved special forces from Mexico’s National Guard and army.

Troops used “stealth and surprise” to establish a security perimeter around a house in Guasave and came under attack with gunfire and explosives before entering and arresting three men, the ministry said.

It identified the other two as German N, known as “Serafin”, the group’s alleged second-in-command, and Jose N, who they identified as a financial operator. The three men were flown to Mexico City and handed over to prosecutors.

Sinaloa’s public security agency urged residents to stay indoors, avoid the area, and stay off the roads, as federal personnel had been attacked in Guasave.

The defence ministry said roadblocks were reported in four areas of Sinaloa after the arrests and that security forces were sent to reopen roads.

Videos from Guasave showed people fleeing gunfire at a baseball game, as well as cars and petrol stations on fire, The Associated Press news agency reported.

Mexico’s security secretary, Omar Garcia Harfuch, said on Saturday that troops would remain in Sinaloa to protect residents.

“These detentions are an important step toward restoring peace in Sinaloa,” he wrote on X.

row: Canada's first climate lawsuit to go to trial has wrapped up hearings. Many more are underway

What level of responsibility does the federal government bear for the climate disasters Canadians are suffering? That's the question at the heart of a landmark lawsuit that wrapped up witness testimony in Federal Court in Vancouver on Friday, and whose outcome could have a big influence on how a growing number of other climate lawsuits in Canada pan out.

Science

# Canada's first climate lawsuit to go to trial has wrapped up hearings. Many more are underway

## Youth lawsuit in Federal Court paves way for other cases questioning governments' duty to ensure safe climate

What level of responsibility does the federal government bear for the climate disasters Canadians are suffering?

That's the question at the heart of a landmark lawsuit that wrapped up witness testimony in Federal Court in Vancouver on Friday, and whose outcome could have a big influence on how a growing number of other climate lawsuits in Canada pan out.

*La Rose et al. v Canada*, brought by 15 youth applicants in 2019 who say the federal government's inadequate actions to reduce carbon emissions is violating their constitutional rights, was heard over the past five weeks — the first full trial for a climate lawsuit in Canada.

A dozen expert witnesses testified, along with the young people themselves.

Andrea Rodgers, deputy director at Our Children's Trust, a legal non-profit that's supporting the case, said it's been "an incredible journey" for the plaintiffs and she hopes the case will inspire "a body of law that will continue to evolve."

"I think if there's one thing many people can agree on, it's that the interests of our children should be prioritized and protected. And this case gives the courts in Canada the opportunity to do that for Canadian youth," Rodgers said Friday.

But even as the historic hearings took place, more cases of climate-related litigation appeared.

On Nov. 18, a <u>lawsuit was filed</u> against the province of Quebec for delaying an emissions target. A <u>lawsuit</u> to force Canada's largest pension fund to better manage climate risk had an important <u>hearing</u> in November.

Two other cases — <u>a youth lawsuit</u> seeking a more stringent climate plan in Ontario and a <u>Federal Court case</u> arguing the federal government is not following its own climate law — are also chugging along.

## **Lawsuits building off each other**

Fraser Thomson, a lawyer at environmental law charity Ecojustice, said as the various cases have gone through the court system, they've "built off each other" by winning legal arguments to pave the way for following cases.

"As more and more courts look at the indisputable evidence that shows that climate change poses an existential threat, courts are increasingly choosing to entertain these arguments and in some cases to weigh in favour of them on certain legal issues," Thomson said.

Thomson is not involved in *La Rose*, but he is a lawyer for the plaintiffs in a newly filed federal lawsuit, *Maltais et al. v Canada*, as well as a long running Ontario case, *Mathur et al. v Ontario.*

*Mathur* was filed in 2019 after Ontario Premier Doug Ford's government weakened the province's emissions targets. The plaintiffs argued that exposed them to climate harms and violated their constitutional rights to life, liberty and security, as well as equality. The case was initially dismissed by the first level of court, but then sent back for a full hearing by the appeal court.

Right before *Mathur* was to receive a hearing in 2025 , the Ford government repealed the law requiring it to set an emissions target at all,  and the case was put on hold. Thomson said he hopes to be back in front of a judge in early 2027 to get some clarity on the path forward.

A rally outside the International Court of Justice in 2025 ahead of an advisory opinion on what legal obligations nations have to address climate change. (Peter Dejong/The Associated Press)

Meanwhile, *Maltais* targets the government's own Net-Zero Emissions Accountability Act. Thomson said "the law says the government has to have a plan" to set and meet its emissions targets, making it a more straightforward argument in court.

It got an early boost this summer when the judge decided the case could proceed after the government asked for it to be dismissed. The two sides will now exchange written arguments, Thomson said.

## **Evolving climate science boosting cases**

The government's defence in *La Rose* relied, in part, on the fact that Canada's emissions form a very small part of global emissions and therefore it alone cannot turn the tide on global warming.

The government's witnesses helped bolster this argument this past week, speaking about the challenges of influencing the global climate, even though Canada is a major fossil fuel producer.

Andrew Leach, an energy and environmental economist at the University of Alberta, testified that even if Canada stopped exporting millions of barrels of oil per day to the U.S., you couldn't assume "those emissions would not occur" because the U.S. could find that oil elsewhere and consume it anyway.

But those emissions still have a measurable impact, and they have been made clearer through huge improvements in climate science.

In recent years, researchers have been able to attribute specific climate disasters like heat waves and floods to climate change, and link emissions of specific fossil fuel producers to changes in the climate.

"In many situations, people are producing scientific reports from the very governments that they are suing. And, so, it's very difficult to be a lawyer from the government and to challenge the findings of a scientific report prepared by your own client," Thomson said.

The judges at the International Court of Justice as they delivered an advisory opinion on international climate obligations in 2025. (Peter Dejong/The Associated Press)

Camille Martini, a doctoral researcher at Université Laval who studies global climate litigation, said lawsuits abroad have also helped drive the "wave" of cases being filed in Canada.

Martini also pointed to the importance of a <u>legal opinion</u> released by the International Court of Justice (ICJ) last year, which said countries have a legal duty to address climate change under international law.

Later, Canada co-sponsored a non-binding resolution in the UN's General Assembly supporting the ICJ's opinion. The resolution was adopted with a vast majority of countries in favour.

"The ICJ opinion clarified … It's really binding on states to do the utmost possible based on each state's capabilities," Martini said, meaning countries can't say they don't have to act because their own emissions are too small.

"So, I think now is the time for Canada to face the music."

Lawyers for both sides in the *La Rose* case will return to court in February, where they will have a week to make their closing statements.

row: FBI probes suspected hack of US crime database

The FBI is investigating a suspected cyberattack on its National Crime Information Centre, a database used by US police, CNN reports. Who is behind it is u Read More: https://punchng.com/fbi-probes-suspected-hack-of-us-crime-database/

The Federal Bureau of Investigation is “investigating a suspected cyberattack on its National Crime Information Centre (NCIC), a nationwide database used by law enforcement agencies across the United States to share criminal justice information.”

The suspected intrusion was discovered in recent days, with two people briefed on the investigation telling CNN that hackers apparently gained access to the system.

The development, reported by CNN on Friday, marks the second reported cyber intrusion involving FBI systems in recent months.

KCRA3 on Saturday reported that a former FBI cybercrime investigations official (name withheld) warned CNN that the concern was not “merely whether hackers accessed sensitive information, but whether they could compromise the accuracy of records used by police officers.

The NCIC serves as a central information-sharing platform for federal, state and local law enforcement agencies, providing access to records on outstanding warrants, wanted individuals, criminal histories and information used for background checks.

A former FBI official who previously led investigations into cybercriminal groups told CNN that the database was critical to day-to-day policing, as officers across the country rely on it to identify wanted fugitives and check outstanding warrants.

The former official also raised concerns about the possibility of hackers compromising the accuracy of information contained in the database, warning that incorrect records could affect decisions made by law enforcement officers.

The FBI did not immediately respond to requests for comment from CNN and Reuters.

The suspected breach comes amid growing concerns over cybersecurity vulnerabilities affecting US government institutions and critical infrastructure, following a series of technological disruptions involving banks, the National Security Agency and the Federal Aviation Administration’s air traffic control systems.

On Thursday, after FBI officials had reportedly learnt of the suspected intrusion, FBI Director Kash Patel appeared on Fox News to discuss the bureau’s cybersecurity efforts.

Patel promoted Operation Winter Shield, an initiative aimed at encouraging organisations to strengthen their digital security and protect critical infrastructure.

“Other administrations could have made these updates, but they didn’t,” he said, “We are staying ahead of the curve and making up for lost time.”

In a separate post on X on Friday, Patel said the FBI was taking the fight against cybercriminals around the world under President Donald Trump’s leadership.

“Through Operation Winter Shield, we’re going on offense against cyber threats, strengthening our nation’s defences, and working with our partners to protect American businesses, government systems, and critical infrastructure,” he wrote.

The latest suspected intrusion follows a September breach of an FBI recruitment website by the digital extortion group ShinyHunters, which reportedly exposed personal information belonging to current and former bureau employees.

The group claimed responsibility for that attack, which prompted an FBI investigation.

However, the “identity of those responsible for the latest suspected intrusion, the method used to access the NCIC and whether any information was stolen or altered remain unclear.”

row: US midterms 2026: What happens before the new Congress takes office?
What happens between the US midterm elections and January, when Democrats take control of Congress?

# US midterms 2026: What happens before the new Congress takes office?

*What happens between the US midterm elections and January, when Democrats take control of Congress?*

The United States midterm elections are over, and the Democrats have won control of both houses of Congress. However, they do not take power until January.

Election officials are still certifying results, while the newly elected lawmakers are preparing to take office, and the outgoing Congress is continuing its legislative work.

So what happens between now and January, and what will change as the 120th Congress takes office?

## What has happened so far?

After the elections, officials have been finalising the results and completing the certification process, which varies by state.

On November 9, the existing Congress returned to Washington for what is known as the “lame-duck” session.

A lame-duck session occurs when Congress meets after an election but before the new Congress takes office.

This means the Republicans still have the majority in both chambers of Congress and can continue passing legislation until the new Congress takes office in January.

## November-December: New lawmakers prepare to take office

During this time, newly elected members start preparing to take office in January.

They attend orientation sessions in Washington, hire staff, and learn more about how Congress operates day-to-day.

Political parties also choose their leaders in the House of Representatives and the Senate. The party controlling each chamber selects the majority leader, while the other party selects the minority leader. The House will also vote on a speaker, who leads the House leadership.

The Republican Party has already re-elected John Thune as its Senate leader, entering the final two years of Donald Trump’s presidency.

The election on the Democratic side, however, is shaping up to be more of a fight.

Among Democrats, Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland is challenging Senator and current Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York to be Senate majority leader, with a vote scheduled for December 1.

Speaking on Al Jazeera’s *This Is America*, Democratic strategist Roger Fisk suggested that the differences between the two candidates may be more about their methods than their political goals.

“I think the difference would probably come in the how rather than the what,” Fisk said.

Republican strategist Doug Heye said the leadership debate reflects wider questions facing both parties after the midterms.

“Both parties have somewhat of an identity crisis,” he said, referring to the Republicans’ losses and the future of the party but also the divisions in the Democratic Party between moderate Democrats and more progressive ones.

## December 11: A government funding deadline

One of the biggest challenges of the current Congress is a December 11 deadline to approve government funding.

Congress passed a temporary spending bill, known as a continuing resolution, to keep the federal agencies functioning without approving a full-year budget.

But before the measure expires, Congress must approve another bill to keep the government funded.

If lawmakers do not reach a deal, part of the federal government could face a shutdown.

Speaking to Al Jazeera, Heye suggested a temporary funding extension could push negotiations into February, by which time Democrats will control both chambers.

“So that would probably go through February,” he said, referring to a possible continuing resolution.

Heye also said the federal debt ceiling is another challenge for the new Congress.

“These are two things that never come up on the campaign trail, but it can be very important to tell us about the next two years,” he added.

## December 17-18: Congress wraps up

The current Congress is expected to finalise its legislative work before the Christmas holidays.

The House’s final sitting day is planned for December 17 and the Senate’s for December 18.

But lawmakers could remain in Washington longer if major issues remain unresolved.

Even if lawmakers finish their work earlier, the 119th Congress’s term does not officially end until January 3.

## January 3, 2027: The new Congress takes power

The 120th Congress starts its term at noon (17:00 GMT) on January 3, 2027.

But January 3 falls on a Sunday, and Congress could pass a law setting a different date for the first meeting.

When the new House convenes, lawmakers must elect a Speaker before being sworn in. Newly elected senators will also take their oaths.

With Democrats controlling both chambers, they will gain authority over congressional committees, legislative priorities and investigations into the administration of President Donald Trump.

“You’re going to have in the House and the Senate something called committee chairs, and they’re all going to be Democrats, and they’re all going to have subpoena power,” Heye told Al Jazeera.

However, he warned that congressional investigations could complicate negotiations between Democrats and the White House.

## What changes politically in January?

Trump will remain president after the midterms, but he will face a Congress controlled by Democrats in both chambers.

This means his administration will have to negotiate with the Democrats to pass legislation, while a Democrat-led Senate will control the confirmation process for presidential nominees.

Democrats will also be able to launch congressional investigations and hold hearings looking at the president’s actions and the actions of those in his inner circle and administration.

House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries has already outlined some of the party’s priorities.

“We need to end the war of choice in Iran. We need to stop the Trump tariffs,” he said.

He also called for reversing Medicaid and food assistance cuts and extending Affordable Care Act tax credits.

But Democratic control of Congress does not guarantee those policies will become law. Trump can veto legislation, while overriding a presidential veto requires a two-thirds majority in both chambers.

“I would hope that \[…\] each side would at least be willing to give each other 60 to 90 days to see where they might be able to cobble together a couple wins on behalf of the American people,” Fisk, the Democratic strategist, said.
